why: This is two-sum counting over distinct value pairs: a pair is identified by its values, not its positions. Put the values in a Counter, and for each distinct value v with v <= target - v, count the pair if its partner exists (needing two copies when v == target - v).
hints: Duplicates must not create extra pairs: (9, 3) counts once even with two 3s. So what is a pair really identified by?
Work over distinct values. For each value v, its partner is target - v. Count the pair once by only counting when v <= target - v.
Counter of values in O(n); loop over its keys, add 1 when the partner is present (and when v == target - v, only if v occurs at least twice). O(n) time and space.
pitfalls: When target is even, the pair (target/2, target/2) needs at least two copies of target/2.
Count each unordered pair once, not twice (once from each side).
n is up to 5 * 10^5, so an O(n^2) pair scan times out.
